extracted.intended_audience: cartoonists, comics artists, humor writers, and readers interested in cartoon craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for making successful cartoons for different platforms (The New Yorker vs Instagram), covering tone, structure, relatability, formal constraints, and production workflow. Useful for cartoonists and humorists refining work for publication or social media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Successful Instagram cartoon — strong emotion and relatability
rubrics_metrics.description: “A good Instagram cartoon, like the ones in Excuse Me, is something that is a strong emotion, that is relatively universal. Let’s say one out of three people can relate to it, rather than one out of fifteen.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for cartoons that express a strong, relatively universal emotion so a substantial fraction of viewers (rough guideline: ~1/3) can relate. Instagram pieces should often feel personally about the viewer (’feel like they’re about you’).

rubrics_metrics.name: New Yorker cartoon — universal, sonnet-like economy and volta
rubrics_metrics.description: “I was talking about New Yorker cartoons when I said that. I also compare them to playing scales—the limitations are very clear and you know how to do it. … They also share a sense of economy, a sonnet being fourteen lines.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For magazine/one-panel markets like The New Yorker, favor universality, precision, an economy of form, and a volta/redirection — analogous to a sonnet's turn. Work to produce one- or two-part comedic structures that are tight and formally disciplined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instagram cartoons as haiku — flash, single punch, personal
rubrics_metrics.description: “I don’t think of the Instagram cartoons as sonnets, I think of them as haikus. They come in a flash and they’re not usually one-two punches like The New Yorker cartoons; they’re just a single punch.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Instagram cartoons as short, immediate flashes that land with a single punchline and often draw from personal feeling; brevity and immediacy are strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance levity and depth; emotional register
rubrics_metrics.description: The book … is earnest and vulnerable but remains very funny. … If you care too much, then you can’t tell a story that moves. You can’t be funny. If you’re too close to something, sometimes you can’t make it light or snappy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive to balance vulnerability/seriousness with humor. Too much emotional closeness can prevent lightness and comedic distance; conversely, levity without depth can feel hollow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two approaches to making a thing worthwhile: step back vs step forward
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation from a cartoon: 'Two ways to make a thing worthwhile: 1. Step backward and find the humor in it. 2. Step forward and find the meaning in it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consciously choose whether a piece's value comes from extracting humor via distance (step back) or from diving into meaning/emotion (step forward); both are valid and produce different effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of unexpected redirection/subversion (volta)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cartoons share a sense of the unexpected, a sonnet requiring a volta, where there’s some kind of redirection or subversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design cartoons around an element of surprise or redirection (the turn) that reframes the setup — this is a core mechanism of effective cartoon humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and formal constraints aid creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: “The limitations are very clear and you know how to do it. If it doesn’t come, at least I know what I’m failing at.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use format constraints (panel size, word economy) to focus creativity; constraints help avoid paralysis that comes from too many options when working at larger scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relatability metric (quantitative guideline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative relatability guideline: aim for roughly one out of three people to relate rather than one out of fifteen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use relatability as a heuristic for broader appeal: more universally accessible emotions/subjects increase potential resonance on platforms like Instagram.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obscurity; clarity to reduce hostile reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: “People tend to write nasty comments when I do something obscure. If people look at something obscure very quickly, they just read it as an attack; I think they’re prepared for an attack.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious with obscure references or insider jokes on fast-consumption platforms — they can be misread as attacks and provoke negative responses. Provide enough context or aim for clearer universality if broad engagement is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: sharp but not bitter; directness equals funniness
rubrics_metrics.description: “It’s sharp but not bitter. It can be funny, it can be direct; I think those are interchangeable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for sharpness and clarity in tone without tipping into bitterness; directness often serves comedic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production/workflow: redrawing, scale, layout, and craft
rubrics_metrics.description: She redrew all the cartoons, scanned them high-resolution and blew them up. For Instagram each drawing is an inch or two; for the book she retraced and did page layout work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in production: redraw and clean sketches for print, scan at high resolution, consider scale and layout. Treat compulsion and volume as part of the craft — high output plus editing/curation matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punch structure differences: single punch vs one-two punch
rubrics_metrics.description: Instagram cartoons: 'they’re just a single punch.' New Yorker cartoons: 'they’re not usually one-two punches like The New Yorker cartoons.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match joke architecture to venue: Instagram favors single, immediate punches; some magazine cartoons can sustain a set-up and secondary turn (one-two).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyzing humor can diminish enjoyment
rubrics_metrics.description: “When we hear a joke we just get still like a dog who smells an animal. It becomes about isolating the part that’s funny and unexpected and thinking more about that. You get spiraled into the nuances of what makes something funny… It stops your enjoyment of some jokes, because some aren’t funny when you think about them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that over-analysis of a joke can reduce its spontaneity and audience enjoyment; sometimes preserving the immediate, unexamined effect is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter nuance: consider local/contextual knowledge and potential to offend
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: posts about 'Park Slope parents and their huge strollers' provoked strong reactions; some readers from other places or parents interpreted the cartoons differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drawing on specific communities or local phenomena, anticipate varied audience perspectives; lack of shared context can lead to misunderstanding or offense — use nuance or frame carefully.
